notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 47 from the sources accessed, organized by verse.

---

## Title and Setting

The psalm is attributed to "the sons of Korah" and dedicated to "the choirmaster." Most commentators agree the sons of Korah were Levitical singers in temple worship, possibly performers rather than authors. Spurgeon believed David was the author and the sons of Korah simply sang it: “Our ear has grown accustomed to the ring of David's compositions, and we are morally certain that we hear it in this Psalm.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

The historical occasion is debated. Proposals include: Jehoshaphat's victory (2 Chronicles 20), the bringing of the ark to Zion (2 Samuel 6), Hezekiah's defeat of the Philistines, or the return from exile. Ellicott notes that “some public rejoicing for victory evidently gave it birth, but whether it was that of Jehoshaphat…or of Hezekiah…or of John Hyrcanus over the Idumæans…must remain in the region of conjecture.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/47.htm)

All traditional Christian interpreters read the psalm as Messianic, looking forward to Christ's ascension and universal reign. The Cambridge Bible notes it “has naturally, on account of Psalm 47:5, been used from ancient times as a special Psalm for Ascension Day.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/47.htm)

---

## v. 1: “Clap your hands, all you peoples; shout unto God with a voice of triumph.”

**Traditional reading:** The psalm opens with two imperatives commanding all nations — not just Israel — to praise God with enthusiastic, bodily expressions of joy. Clapping hands draws attention and is an outward expression of inward joy. Spurgeon: “If they cannot all speak the same tongue, the symbolic language of the hands they can all use.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

David Guzik notes that “most people are not against shouting or enthusiastic outbursts; they simply believe there is a right and wrong place for such shouting. Sadly, many who think a loud exclamation is fine at a football game think it is a scandal in the church.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

Matthew Henry, cited by Spurgeon, cautions that “such expressions of pious and devout affection as to some may seem indecent and imprudent, yet ought not to be hastily censured…because if they come from an upright heart, God will accept the strength of the affection, and excuse the weakness of the expressions of it.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

Gill reads “all ye people” as meaning “the Gentiles more especially,” since the ascended Lord was given as their Saviour and the gospel was now preached among them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-47.html)

Adam Clarke (Methodist) observed four aspects of this praise: it should be cheerful (clapping), universal (all peoples), vocal (shout), and frequent. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

**Reformed view (Ligonier):** The call to “all peoples” demonstrates that the OT is a missionary book. Ancient Near Eastern peoples assumed gods were territorial, but Psalm 47 makes the universal claim that Yahweh is to be worshipped by all nations. These nations must hear of Israel's God if they are to praise Him. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/praising-god-king)

---

## v. 2: “How awesome is the LORD Most High, the great King over all the earth!”

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist presents God's awesomeness as self-evident, needing no proof. “He is a great King” — both His office (King of Kings) and His realm (all the earth) are emphasized. Guzik notes that pagan gods like Baal and Molech were imagined to be territorial, but the LORD is not like these imagined gods: “His realm extends over all the earth, and He is sovereign in all places.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

Spurgeon: “Not over Judea only, but even to the utmost isles his reign extends. Our God is no local deity, no petty ruler of a tribe…Not a hamlet or an islet is excluded from his dominion.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

The word translated “awesome” (or “terrible” in the KJV) means “to be feared.” Spurgeon explains: “Omnipotence, which is terrible to crush, is almighty to protect. At a grand review of the troops of a great prince, all his loyal subjects are filled with triumph, because their liege lord is so able to defend his own, and so much dreaded by his foes.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

**Reformed view (Ligonier):** The title “great King” was a suzerain-vassal treaty term used by emperors over smaller states. By casting Yahweh as the “great King” (suzerain) of the whole earth, the psalmist calls the world to serve the God of Israel and no other — pledging absolute loyalty to Him. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/praising-god-king)

**Lange's Commentary** emphasizes the Messianic dimension: “God is the governor of the whole world…His omnipotent acts prove that He rules in all lands.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/psalms-47.html)

---

## v. 3: “He subdues nations beneath us, and peoples under our feet.”

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist speaks as one of God's chosen nation, looking forward to the time when Israel would assume leadership among the nations under Messiah's reign. Spurgeon reads it as the church's spiritual conquest: “Idolatry, infidelity, superstition, we shall yet tread upon, as men tread down the stones of the street…The church of God shall be the greatest of monarchies, her victory shall be signal and decisive.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

Gill interprets this spiritually: the conquest is by the gospel, not the sword. Through the apostles' preaching, Gentiles became “willing to be saved by him; to submit to his righteousness, and to his ordinances.” The phrase “under our feet” alludes to sitting at the feet of a teacher — the Gentiles becoming learners under Jewish apostles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-47.html)

George Horne (cited by Spurgeon): “The consequence of our Lord's ascension was the going forth of the all-subduing Word…the convinced and converted nations renounced their idols and their lusts, and bowed their willing necks to the yoke of Jesus.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

**Pulpit Commentary** stresses that the subjugation cannot be a carnal one, because the nations are invited to “clap their hands” at it — it is “the yearning of men's minds and hearts for God.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/47.htm)

---

## v. 4: “He chooses our inheritance for us, the pride of Jacob, whom He loves. Selah”

**Traditional reading:** The psalmist expresses contentment in letting God choose his people's inheritance — both the land of Canaan (“the pride of Jacob” or “Jacob's glorious land,” as Kidner puts it) and ultimately their eternal inheritance in Christ. Guzik expands this to our calling, our blessings, and even our crosses: “We sometimes want to choose our own crosses. We think that our own problems are so much worse than others…except the one He chose for us.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

Spurgeon: “This is the most spiritual and real manner of clapping our hands because of his sovereignty, namely, to leave all our affairs in his hands, for then our hands are empty of all care for self, and free to be used in his honour.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

William Secker (Puritan, cited by Spurgeon): “Never were any their own carvers, but they were sure to cut their own fingers.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

“Selah” marks a musical pause for meditation. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

**Reformed view:** John Calvin comments that the kingdom of God “would be much more magnificent and glorious at the coming of the Messiah, than it was under the shadowy dispensation of the Law, inasmuch as it would be extended to the utmost boundaries of the earth.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/praising-god-king)

**Spurgeon's sermon on this verse** (July 8, 1855) emphasizes that the Christian is pleased when he can “see Christ in the Scriptures” and that leaving one's inheritance to God's choice is the essence of faith. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/psalms-47.html)

---

## v. 5: “God has ascended amid shouts of joy, the LORD with the sound of the horn.”

**Traditional reading:** This is the verse that has made Psalm 47 the “Ascension Psalm” in Christian liturgy. The “going up” refers to ascending to a royal throne after victory. Spurgeon: “The fight is over, the conqueror ascends to his triumphant chariot…The words are fully applicable to the ascension of the Redeemer…Fresh from Bozrah, with his garments all red from the winepress, he ascended, leading captivity captive.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

Guzik explains: “The idea is that God comes down from heaven to help and save His people, and when He goes back up to heaven, He deserves praise and acclamation…Jesus ascended the royal throne in heaven after He finished His work for us on the cross.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

Gill notes that ancient Jewish sources themselves (Bemidbar Rabba) applied this verse to the Messiah. He also observes that although the NT account of the ascension does not mention a trumpet, the angels said Christ would descend as He ascended, and His descent will be “with the trump of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-47.html)

**Cambridge Bible** makes an important distinction: the verse in context does not originally refer to Christ's ascension into heaven but to God ascending to His throne after triumph — yet the words “may be legitimately applied to the return of Christ to heaven after His triumph over sin and death.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/47.htm)

**Ellicott** sees the “going up” not as going to heaven but “as in Psalms 24, to the Temple, as is shown by the public acclaim accompanying the ark to its resting-place after victory.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/47.htm)

**Old & New Testament Restoration Commentary** argues that this is a direct prophecy: “God's ‘going up’ in this passage is a prophetic reference to the Ascension to heaven of our Lord Jesus Christ. That is the reason that Christian scholars for centuries have called this ‘One of the Ascension Psalms.’” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-47.html)

**Andrew Bonar** (Free Church of Scotland, cited by Spurgeon) offered a different view: “Some have applied this Psalm to Christ's ascension; but it speaks of his Second Coming. The Mighty One is seated peacefully on his throne.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

---

## vv. 6–7: “Sing praises to God, sing praises; sing praises to our King, sing praises! For God is King of all the earth; sing profound praises to Him.”

**Traditional reading:** The command to sing praises appears five times in rapid succession, conveying urgency and intensity. Spurgeon: “What jubilation is here, when five times over the whole earth is called upon to sing to God!…Sing praises, keep on with the glad work. Never let the music pause.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

Adam Clarke: “This word is four times repeated in this short verse, and shows at once the earnestness and happiness of the people.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

“Sing profound praises” (BSB) or “sing praises with understanding” (KJV) — literally *maskil*, a didactic or skillful psalm. Guzik explains: “God wants our worship to be intelligent and not mindless. It is not necessary to be smart to worship God, but we should worship Him with all our being, including our mind (Mark 12:30).” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

Spurgeon is particularly pointed: “We must not be guided by the time, but the words of the Psalm; we must mind the matter more than the music, and consider what we sing, as well as how we sing; the tune may affect the fancy, but it is the matter affects the heart.” He warns against “a sensuous delight in organs, anthems” that substitutes physical effects for spiritual impulses. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

Ellicott translates “Sing praises” as “Strike the harp,” and “with understanding” as “play a fine tune” or “play with skill.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/47.htm)

**Reformed (Ligonier):** The repeated call to sing praises reinforces that God is “King of all the earth” — not just Israel's God but the global sovereign to whom all owe allegiance. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/praising-god-king)

---

## v. 8: “God reigns over the nations; God is seated on His holy throne.”

**Traditional reading:** God's reign is not passive or ceremonial — He actively governs history. Guzik: “God sits upon the throne; it is not empty. He is not an empty or ceremonial ruler…It is a holy throne, where the holiness of God has been perfectly satisfied by the work of Jesus on the cross. Therefore, it is both a holy throne and a throne of grace (Hebrews 4:16).” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

Spurgeon: “Now at this moment, over the most debased idolaters, God holds a secret rule; here is work for faith…Unmoved he occupies an undisputed throne, whose decrees, acts, and commands are holiness itself. What other throne is like this? Never was it stained with injustice, or defiled with sin.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

Gill notes two aspects: God's present reign over the Gentiles through gospel conversions, and His future visible reign when “the kingdoms of this world will become his.” He ties this directly to Christ seated at the right hand of God after His ascension. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-47.html)

The **Pulpit Commentary** emphasizes that “the mediatorial throne is ‘the throne of his holiness’…In the life of Christ holiness was manifested; in his death, whereby he condemned sin, holiness was vindicated. From his seat above, holiness sways the sceptre.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/47.htm)

---

## v. 9: “The nobles of the nations have assembled as the people of the God of Abraham; for the shields of the earth belong to God; He is highly exalted.”

**Traditional reading:** The psalm culminates in a vision of Gentile princes gathered together with Israel to worship the one true God — the fulfillment of the Abrahamic promise that “all nations shall be blessed” through his seed. Spurgeon: “How august will be the parliament where the Lord Jesus shall open the court, and princes shall rise up to do him honour!…Babel's dispersion shall be obliterated by the gathering arm of the Great Shepherd King.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

Guzik, citing Kidner: “It is the abundant fulfillment of the promise of Genesis 12:3; it anticipates what Paul expounds of the inclusion of the Gentiles as Abraham's sons (Romans 4:11; Galatians 3:7-9).” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

The “shields of the earth” is understood figuratively. Spurgeon: “The insignia of pomp, the emblems of rank, the weapons of war, all must pay loyal homage to the King of all. Those who are earth's protectors, the shields of the commonwealth, derive their might from him, and are his.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)

The Septuagint translates “shields” as *hoi krataioi* — “the strong ones of the earth” — meaning rulers or princes. Clarke says the phrase may also refer to “God's providence, guardian angels, etc.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

Gill interprets “the princes of the people” as “the willing or voluntary ones” (connecting to Psalm 110:3) — those made willing by grace to submit to Christ. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-47.html)

**Pulpit Commentary:** “All the nations are under Immanuel's sceptre…‘In Christ there is neither Greek, nor Jew, barbarian, Scythian, bond, nor free; but Christ is all, and in all.’ And in him all the peoples of the earth may find their home in Abraham's God.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/47.htm)

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Distinctives

**Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill, Garner-Howes):** Strong emphasis on the church's spiritual conquest through gospel preaching (not literal warfare), individual submission of the will (“He shall choose our inheritance for us”), and Christ's ascension as the interpretive key for the whole psalm. The repeated “sing praises” is taken as a call to heartfelt, doctrinally-informed worship. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-47.html)

**Reformed (Ligonier, Calvin):** Emphasis on God's universal sovereignty using suzerain-vassal treaty language, the OT as a missionary book, and the expansion of God's kingdom to all nations through the Messiah as far more glorious than the “shadowy dispensation of the Law.” (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/praising-god-king)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Enthusiastic, demonstrative praise (clapping, shouting) is affirmed as biblically appropriate for the church today. Guzik directly critiques those who accept loud celebration at sporting events but consider it scandalous in church. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-47/)

**Anglican (Ellicott, Cambridge, Pulpit):** More cautious on prophetic interpretation. Cambridge notes that v. 5 does not in its original context prophesy Christ's ascension but may be applied to it legitimately. Ellicott reads “gone up” as referring to the Temple, not heaven. The Pulpit Commentary, however, sees the psalm's terms as “intelligible only as referred immediately to the conflict and victory of the great Captain of salvation.” (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/47.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/47.htm; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/psalms/47.htm)

**Older Anglican (Simeon):** Reads the psalm as David's celebration of the ark's ascent to Zion, typologically foreshadowing Christ's ascension. “On his very cross he spoiled all the principalities and powers of darkness, triumphing over them openly in it.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/shh/psalms-47.html)

**Andrew Bonar (Free Church of Scotland, noted by Spurgeon):** Dissents from the ascension reading, arguing the psalm speaks of Christ's *Second Coming* — “The Mighty One is seated peacefully on his throne.” (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps047.php)
